p: Writing is the boundary of my profession. Before it lies prehistory, the province of the digger and the naturalist; after it lies history proper, in which we may hear people speak for themselves. It is the invention that allows the dead to address the living, the absent to address the present, and the king to address the farthest province of his empire in his own words. It is also, I must add, the invention that made possible the tax return, the bill of sale, and the warrant for arrest, and it was for such things that it was first employed.

The oldest true writing that we know arose in Mesopotamia, in the city of Uruk, a little more than five thousand years ago. It did not begin as a means of recording speech. It began as a means of keeping accounts. For thousands of years before, the people of the Near East had used little tokens of baked clay, in various shapes, to stand for quantities of goods: a cone for a measure of grain, a disc for a sheep, and so on. At some point, it seems, people began sealing such tokens inside hollow balls of clay as a guarantee of a transaction, and pressing the tokens into the outside of the ball first, so that the contents could be known without breaking it. Then someone realised that the marks on the outside were sufficient, and the tokens inside unnecessary. This, at least, is the theory of an American scholar, Denise Schmandt-Besserat, which the Encyclopaedia reports with due caution. It has the great merit of explaining why the earliest tablets are almost entirely lists of goods, rations and labourers.

The scribes of Uruk drew their signs at first as little pictures, scratched into soft clay with a pointed stick. In time they found it quicker to press the signs in with the cut end of a reed, which leaves a wedge-shaped mark, and the pictures became patterns of wedges. We call this writing cuneiform, from the Latin word cuneus, meaning a wedge. The crucial step came when the scribes began to use signs for their sounds rather than their meanings. The Sumerian word for arrow, for instance, sounded like the word for life, so the sign for an arrow could be used to write life. This is the principle of the rebus, the picture-puzzle in which a drawing of a bee and a leaf spells belief, and it is the key that unlocked the writing of whole sentences, names, poems and laws.

Writing was invented, the Encyclopaedia tells me, at least three or four times independently. In Egypt, the hieroglyphs, which means sacred carvings in Greek, appeared at much the same time as cuneiform, or a little later; whether the Egyptians took the idea from Mesopotamia or arrived at it themselves is still disputed. In China, the oldest writing we possess is found on the bones of oxen and the shells of tortoises used for divination under the Shang kings, about three thousand two hundred years ago; the king would put a question to the spirits, heat the bone until it cracked, read the answer in the cracks, and have the question and sometimes the answer carved beside them. Those characters are the direct ancestors of the Chinese writing used today, which makes it the longest continuous tradition of writing in the world. And in Mexico and Central America, the Maya and their neighbours developed a writing of great beauty and complexity, which the scholars of the twentieth century, after long frustration, at last learned to read.

All these early writings required the learning of hundreds or thousands of signs, and they were therefore the property of a small class of trained scribes. The great simplification came with the alphabet. Somewhere about three thousand eight hundred years ago, people speaking a Semitic language, perhaps workers or soldiers in the Egyptian territory of Sinai, took a handful of Egyptian pictures and used each of them for the first sound of its name in their own tongue. The picture of an ox, called aleph, stood for the sound at the beginning of aleph; the picture of a house, called bet, for the sound b. From this beginning came, by many stages, the alphabet of the Phoenicians, those great traders of the coast of Lebanon, who carried it across the Mediterranean. The Greeks took it from them, adding signs for the vowels, which the Phoenicians had not written; and the very word alphabet is made of the names of its first two Greek letters, alpha and beta, which are the old aleph and bet. From the Greeks it passed to the Etruscans and the Romans, and from the Romans to us. When you hear a capital A, you hear, at four thousand years' distance, an ox turned upside down.

With an alphabet of two or three dozen letters, reading could be learned by almost anyone. It did not follow that almost anyone learned it. For most of history the great majority of people, in every land, could not read. In my own England, at the time of my birth, perhaps half of the men and fewer of the women could sign their names in the marriage register. The Elementary Education Act of eighteen seventy, five years ago, has begun at last to provide a school for every child, and I live in hope of a nation that reads.

Writing did not merely record speech; it changed thought. A spoken argument vanishes; a written one can be examined, compared and criticised at leisure. Laws written down can be appealed to against the whim of a judge. Histories written down can be checked against one another, which is the whole foundation of my trade. Writing made possible the great religions of the book, the long arguments of philosophy, the slow accumulation of science. It allowed knowledge to outlive the knower.

Yet I would not have you think that the peoples without writing were without learning. They kept their laws, their genealogies and their sacred stories in memory, and the poems of Homer were, very probably, composed and handed down by singers who could not read. Plato, in a dialogue called the Phaedrus, records the complaint of an Egyptian king that writing would destroy the memory of those who learned it, and give them the appearance of wisdom without the reality. There is truth in that complaint, as anyone who has examined an undergraduate will agree. But it is a complaint which we know only because Plato wrote it down.
